readerTitle: The 50/50 handshake that felt fair on day one
caseNote: 가상 사례 (케이터링 창업, 물류 회사의 소프트웨어 팀 분사) + 실제 연구 (Wasserman, Hellmann & Wasserman)
insight: 창업자 지분은 아이디어나 첫날의 기여에 대한 보상이 아니라, 앞으로 몇 년간 할 일에 대한 대가다.
misconception: 친구끼리 똑같이 나누는 것이 가장 공정하다. 아이디어를 낸 사람이 가장 많이 가져야 한다.

sources.text: Wasserman, N. (2012). The Founder's Dilemmas. Princeton University Press.
Hellmann, T. & Wasserman, N. (2017). The First Deal: The Division of Founder Equity in New Ventures. Management Science.
케이터링과 물류 회사 분사 사례는 설명용 가상 사례

factChecks.note: Hellmann & Wasserman(2017)의 결론을 5번 카드에 일반적으로만 적었습니다. '균등 분할이 흔하다', '빠르게 합의한 균등 분할 팀이 이후 투자 유치에서 불리한 경향' 두 문장이 논문 결과와 맞는지 원문으로 확인하세요. 구체적 비율은 일부러 넣지 않았습니다.
Wasserman 연구가 '수천 개 미국 스타트업' 데이터에 기반한다는 표현이 책·논문의 표본 설명과 맞는지 확인하세요.
케이터링 사례의 $10,000, 주 60시간 등은 모두 가상 수치입니다. 계산은 없습니다.
법률·세무 조언으로 읽히지 않도록 7번 카드에 '전문가와 서면 합의' 정도만 적었습니다. 국가별 법률 내용은 넣지 않았습니다.

cards.title: The 50/50 handshake that felt fair on day one
body: Two friends open a catering business. Over coffee, they agree to split it 50/50. It takes ten minutes.
It's the fastest decision they'll make together. Two years later, it's the one they argue about most.

image.label: Two hands shaking over a coffee table with a pie chart split in half
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 카페 테이블 위에서 두 사람이 악수하고, 테이블 위에 정확히 반으로 나뉜 파이 차트가 놓여 있음. 한쪽 그림자에 살짝 금이 간 느낌. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: How should Maya and Jon split the business?
body: Maya had the idea and puts in $10,000. She'll keep her day job for now and handle sales on weekends.
Jon is a chef. He'll quit his job and cook full-time from the first week. How should they split ownership?

options.feedback: It's fast and avoids an awkward talk. But it prices today's friendship, not the very different amounts of work each will do next.

options.text: Maya gets 60%, for the idea and the cash
options.feedback: Her money and risk deserve credit. But the cash could be treated as a loan, and an idea is worth little until someone builds it.

options.text: First agree who will do what over the next three or four years, then split
options.feedback: It takes longer and may feel uncomfortable. It's the only option that looks at where the business's value will actually come from.

cards.title: Both of them were right. The split wasn't.
body: They chose 50/50. Two years in, Jon works 60-hour weeks in the kitchen. Maya still works part-time on sales.
Jon feels he's building half of Maya's company for free. Maya feels she took the real risk with her savings and deserves her half.
Each has a fair point. The handshake priced neither of them. It was a quick guess about a future no one had discussed.

cards.title: Ownership pays for the future
body: **Splitting ownership** means deciding what share of the business each founder holds. Most of that share is payment for work not yet done.
On day one, a new business is worth very little. Almost all its value gets created later, by whoever does the work.
So the useful question isn't "who got us here?" It's **"who will build what from here?"** Money put in can be handled separately, for example as a loan or a stake bought for cash.

image.label: Timeline: a tiny day-one block and a large block of future value
image.brief: 가로 타임라인 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 'Day one'에는 아주 작은 블록(아이디어, 초기 자금), 오른쪽으로 갈수록 'Year 1', 'Year 2', 'Year 3' 블록이 커짐. 큰 블록마다 일하는 사람 아이콘. 지분은 대부분 오른쪽 블록에 대한 대가라는 메시지.

cards.title: Quick equal splits are common, and costly.
body: Harvard researcher Noam Wasserman studied founding teams across thousands of US startups for his book *The Founder's Dilemmas*.

In later work with Thomas Hellmann, he found that equal splits are common and are often agreed quickly. Teams that split equally with little discussion tended to do worse when they later raised money.
The lesson isn't that equal is wrong. It's that a split no one thought hard about is a guess, and guesses get tested when the work starts piling up.

cards.title: What to weigh, from most to least
body: When founders talk it through, these usually matter in this order.

breakdown.label: Future time
breakdown.detail: Full-time or part-time, and for how long

breakdown.label: Role
breakdown.detail: How hard that person would be to replace

breakdown.label: Risk taken
breakdown.detail: Salary given up, money put in

breakdown.label: The idea
breakdown.detail: Worth little until someone builds it

cards.callout: The idea feels biggest on day one. It matters least by year three.

cards.title: No formula gives the right number.
body: Equal can be exactly right when founders really will commit the same time and carry similar roles. And haggling for weeks over a few points can damage trust before you start.
The bigger problem: a split based on future work is only fair if that work actually happens. People change jobs, get sick or lose interest. That's what **vesting**, the next lesson, is for.
Whatever you agree, write it down properly with expert help.

cards.title: Now it's a team inside a bigger company.
body: A logistics company's internal team of four built route-planning software. The company will spin it out as a separate business.
The company gives the software, its first customer contract and a year of funding. The four will leave their jobs to run the new company. How should ownership be split?

options.text: The parent keeps 95%. It paid for everything so far
options.feedback: It fully rewards the past. But the four people doing all the future work have little reason to stay when the work gets hard.

options.text: The team gets a large stake, earned over the coming years. The parent's stake reflects its funding and contract
options.feedback: It pays each side for what it keeps giving. The parent gives up some ownership in exchange for a team that's motivated to build.

options.text: Split evenly among everyone who ever worked on the project, including people staying at the parent
options.feedback: It thanks past helpers fairly. But it hands payment for future work to people who won't be doing it.

cards.softwareNote: In software, nearly all value comes after launch, from years of building and selling. That makes the future-work test even more important than in businesses with big upfront assets.

cards.title: Split ownership by who builds what next.
body: A founder's share is mostly payment for years of work still ahead. Talk through those years before you shake hands.
**Try it today:** if you have partners, write each person's expected hours, role and risk for the next three years beside their current share. Do the two columns match?
